title: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease: A case report
case_prompt: A 62-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department with a 3-month history of progressive cognitive decline, including ataxia, memory loss, and disorientation. She had no prior neurologic illness. On examination, she was alert but disoriented to time and place, with impaired short-term memory and a broad-based gait. Vital signs were normal. Noncontrast CT of the head and CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no evidence of malignancy, infarction, or hemorrhage. Laboratory evaluations—including metabolic panels, infectious and autoimmune encephalitis panels, and toxicology screens—were unremarkable. Brain MRI revealed diffusion restriction and T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the bilateral caudate nuclei, putamen, thalami, hippocampi, and in a gyriform pattern in the bilateral frontal and temporal cortices, without contrast enhancement or mass effect.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infection, metabolic, or autoimmune encephalitis were excluded based on laboratory testing — “Multiple tests were performed to exclude causes such as infection, toxic or metabolic diseases, and autoimmune encephalitis.”  
2. Paraneoplastic encephalitis was considered but imaging and body CT scans were negative for malignancy — “CT of the head and chest/abdomen/pelvis were performed initially, which were negative for malignancy, infarction or hemorrhage.”  
3. Hypoxic–ischemic encephalopathy and other metabolic disorders can mimic MRI findings but were less likely in the absence of a precipitating event and metabolic derangements — “Its specificity is limited due to overlap of imaging findings with other neurologic disorders such as hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy, encephalitis, and metabolic disorders such as hepatic encephalopathy or hypoglycemia.”  
4. The pattern of cortical and basal ganglia diffusion restriction and FLAIR hyperintensity is characteristic of CJD — “In the case of CJD, there is typically diffusion restriction and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity involving the cortex and the basal ganglia (caudate and putamen).”  
5. Sporadic CJD was favored given the absence of risk factors for inherited, iatrogenic, or variant forms — “The most prevalent variety is sporadic, which happens when there are no risk factors present.”  
6. Periodic sharp wave complexes on EEG supported a prionopathy — “As the disease progresses to middle and late stages, the EEG commonly shows periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWCs).”  
7. Elevation of 14-3-3 protein in CSF supported prion disease, despite its limited specificity — “However, these biomarkers are nonspecific and can be increased due to other conditions like Alzheimer's disease, CNS infections, stroke, etc.”  
8. Other progressive dementias such as Alzheimer's disease, Lewy body dementia, and frontotemporal dementia were considered but are less likely given the rapid course and imaging features — “Differential considerations of progressive dementia include many entities such as Alzheimher's disease, Lewy body dementia, frontotemporal dementia, meningoencephalitis, corticobasal degeneration, progressive supranuclear palsy, CADASIL, and paraneoplastic encephalitis.”
